paragraphs: […God] set [its nature] for that act by His positing, and created it by His creating, without its nature having existed beforehand. He compelled it and provided for it until it acted and brought forth. This is among the strongest proofs of the world's origination, and that it is from an Originator who is Himself eternal.[{3}]

What we have just said — that the heavens and the firmament are an indication (dilāla) of the Creator (mighty and exalted) — is the meaning of David's words (peace upon him): "The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament announces the work of His hands" (Ps 19:2 [Heb. 19:2; KJV 19:1]).[{4}] What he means is that the firmament announces this by way of indication, in the same way one says of some object that "it speaks for itself" — meaning that there are in it signs that indicate its meaning. Of the same kind is the saying of Job (peace upon him): "And from my flesh I shall see God" (Job 19:26)[{5}] — meaning, from my body and from myself I see and infer and confirm the Creator (great is His praise): for I was at the outset of my affair a drop of seed that issued from the loins of my father; then I became, in the womb, a clot; then I was given a shape; then organs and members were given to me; then the spirit was breathed into me, and by it I became alive, sensing, moving; then I was brought out of the womb, lacking reason and discrimination; then I came to reason after that as a child; then I passed from infancy to childhood, from childhood to youth, from youth to old age — and in all of this I am compelled, not choosing anything of what I come to be. Since this is the case, it follows clearly from it that I have a Mover[{6}] who moves me from one state to another, from one mode of being to another, and He is the One who created me. This is also among the things by which the Monotheists infer the Creator (mighty and exalted).

Among what is in Scripture commanding baḥth and naẓar — especially in the state of unguidedness (al-jāhiliyya)[{7}] — is the saying of Moses (peace upon him) in the Torah of God: "And it shall come to pass, when all these things shall come upon thee — the blessings and the curses that I have set before thee — and thou shalt return into thy heart among all the nations…" (Deut 30:1).[{8}] He commanded us, in the state of unguidedness, to return into the discrimination of the heart and discriminate between truth and falsehood; and that cannot be except by baḥth and naẓar. What further obligates baḥth and naẓar from Scripture: the saying of David to his son: "And thou, Solomon my son, know the God of thy father and serve Him with a whole heart and a willing soul" (1 Chr 28:9). He commanded knowing before serving — since the one who serves a god he does not know offers no [valid] service. And the knowledge of the Creator (mighty is His praise) can only be by means of the rational faculties. If someone claims that this can be by report — well, the reports about this are at variance; which of them shall we take? It is necessary, of necessity, to return to the rational evidences and demonstrations. What further obligates this is the saying of Jeremiah (peace upon him): "Thus said the Lord: stand ye in the ways and see, and ask for the old paths — which is the good way? — and walk therein" (Jer 6:16). He thus commanded and obligated baḥth and the search by which what is to be chosen is the truth, the better and the more excellent that one walks in and adopts — and that cannot be except by al-ʿaql and al-qiyās. Of the same kind is the saying of Isaiah (peace upon him): "If the wicked is granted favor, he does not learn righteousness" (Isa 26:10)[{9}] — meaning that the transgressor is shown favor while in his transgression, so long as he does not investigate and reflect, and that is at the outset of his career; but when the matter has been long with him, and he has not turned to what is in the earth of admonitions, and he has not reflected on what is in it of the power of the Creator (mighty and exalted), and he has remained heedless — favor departs from him. Do you not see, then, that he has been moved to investigate and reflect? This indicates that if he is heedless of baḥth and naẓar, He does not show him favor. We therefore conclude from this that baḥth and naẓar are obligatory upon him in his very rational faculty.[{10}]

In our book[{11}] there are very many parallels [to these scriptural commands], which I have abstained from enumerating in detail to avoid prolixity, and because what we have mentioned suffices. That, then, is what Scripture mentions concerning the obligation of baḥth, naẓar, and the use of rational analogy [in religious matters]. But as for what falls outside that — what belongs to the genus of inquiry into natural-philosophical matters (al-naẓar fī al-umūr al-falsafiyya al-ṭabīʿiyya) — Scripture too contains indications and reports that refute those who claim that naẓar in these matters is impermissible. Of these: what Scripture reports about Solomon, who employed such inquiry and spoke on it. He says: "And he spoke about the trees, from the cedar that is in Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of the wall" (1 Kgs 5:13 [4:33 in some traditions]). And: "And he spoke about the cattle, and about the birds, and about the creeping things, and about the fish" (1 Kgs 5:13). He reports that Solomon discoursed on all the plants from the smallest to the greatest, and likewise that he discoursed on all the species of animals: of land, air, and sea. What did he have to say about them? In what terms did he discuss them? Can it have been anything but a report on their natures, on their causes (ʿilal), on the beneficial and the harmful in them, and on what is in them of the traces of wisdom? And that on the same plan that the wise men and philosophers spoke, and as is recorded in their books — indeed, Solomon is the original source of it (I mean: from him they took).[{12}] This is one of the clearest proofs that naẓar in natural-philosophical matters is licit and not impermissible; rather, the one who engages in it and reflects on it is better than the one who abandons it. For the one who reflects on these matters, his knowledge of the Creator grows stronger, the wisdom of the Creator (mighty and exalted) becomes evident to him, and his understanding of Scripture is therefore better — since there are things in Scripture whose understanding requires this very inquiry. His desire for religion accordingly grows greater and stronger. [A qualification:] This is the case if the one who undertakes such inquiry is of balanced nature and strong native intellect, and his pursuit is the pursuit of one who desires the knowledge of realities, without partiality or bias. But if his native intellect is feeble and not balanced — if his disposition (naḥīza) is weak — then it is not fitting for him to enter into any of the rational-philosophical sciences. As one of the sages has said: "Some men are corrupted in religion only when they take up subtle sciences with feeble intellects." This is a noble saying in its meaning.[{13}]

Another scriptural indication: what Scripture reports about Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, in the saying: "And in every matter of wisdom and understanding that the king inquired of them, he found them ten times above all the wise men [magicians and astrologers] that were in all his realm" (Dan 1:20). It reports that the king examined them about kinds of wisdom (ḥikma), and that in everything he examined them about he found them ten ranks above his own wise men. The kinds of wisdom and sciences he examined them in must have been the natural-philosophical sciences — it cannot have been otherwise, since the report says they exceeded his wise men by ten ranks in those sciences. This is in the highest degree of confirmation, and contains the clearest proof that the children of Israel were in fact engaged in these sciences — except that it appears that this was the case only among the khawāṣṣ (the elite) among them, like the people of the royal household and the priests. For these four men, and those with them, were of the royal household — as is said at the start of the narrative: "to bring some of the children of Israel, of the seed of the king and the nobles, young men in whom there was no defect, and goodly in appearance, well-versed in every science, who know understanding and grasp it…" (Dan 1:3–4). And like the fathers of the children of Issachar, of whom it is said: "men who had understanding of the times" (1 Chr 12:32).[{14}]

Scripture has touched on, in many places, things from the domain of nature: medicine, the science of the stars, the upper [meteorological] effects, and the like. What it has said in medicine: His saying (Exod 21:19), "He shall pay for his idle time, and shall surely cause him to be healed."[{15}] And His saying (Jer 8:22), "Is there no balm in Gilead?" What it mentioned of the influence of the heavenly bodies: His saying, "And of the precious things put forth by the sun" (Deut 33:14). What is meant is the influence of the sun on the fruits, its ripening of them, and what it produces in them of colors (red, yellow, and so on). And His saying [in the same verse], "and of the precious things brought forth by the moons" — by which the influence of the moon on the cucumber-patches (al-maqātīʾ) and melon-patches (al-mabāṭikh), and the like, is meant — things observed by sense. There is also the saying (Deut 4:19), "Lest thou lift up thine eyes unto heaven, and seeing the sun and the moon and the stars…", together with "…which the Lord thy God hath imparted unto all nations." We will explain this in Maqāla VI, in the discussion of His saying (Exod 20:3), "Thou shalt have no other gods before Me." Likewise concerning the form of the heavenly sphere — that it is like a tent — His saying (Isa 40:22): "He stretches out the heavens as a curtain, and spreads them as a tent for inhabiting." We have explained that in our commentary on the book of Genesis.

He has also reported, on the matter of astronomy, that the sun has two motions: one by which it is moved by the sphere of the constellations, from east to west, in His saying (Eccl 1:5): "And the sun ariseth and the sun goeth down…"; and a second motion proper to the sun itself, from west to east, in His saying [in the same place, v. 6]: "It goeth toward the south and turneth about unto the north." We have made this clear in our commentary on Ecclesiastes and in the commentary on Genesis. He has also indicated the jawzahar[{16}] — which is the Dragon, two nodes in the celestial sphere — in His saying (Job 26:13): "By His Spirit the heavens are made fair; His hand has pierced the fleeing Serpent." We have explained that in our commentary on the book of Job. He has also indicated the standing of the earth in the midst of the celestial sphere, in His saying (Job 26:7): "He hangs the earth upon nothing." He has also indicated some of the upper effects — that rain and all moisture are from vapor rising from the earth — in His saying (Gen 2:6): "And a mist used to rise from the earth, and water all the face of the ground." He has also indicated some of the kinds of natural wisdom placed in animals — among them the saying of Solomon (peace upon him) (Prov 30:24): "Four things are little upon the earth…", and his saying [v. 29 of the same place]: "There be three of stately gait…". Of this kind there is a great deal, of which we have indicated portions in the commentary on Genesis and other commentaries.

There still remain for us proofs for the establishment of qiyās in the farāʾiḍ (the affirmative commandments) — proofs that we have postponed, because some of the muḥdithīn (the latter-day) among the Rabbanites have brought objections to some of them and have attempted to refute qiyās itself. We will mention this and reply to it in its proper place [i.e. in Babs 9 ff.]. We now return to what we promised: namely, what a man must adopt and hold to before he commences baḥth and naẓar.[{17}] ---
